subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF NOVA SCOTIA LOBSTER FISHERMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a statement regarding the Shelburne County enforcement crisis. By condoning the oppressive crackdown on lobster fishermen in southwestern Nova Scotia, the present Liberal Government is once again demonstrating its insensitivity to the need for Canadians in small communities to retain their dignity and economic self-determination.
These fishermen are being unfairly attacked because they were honest enough to inform the Government that the lobster trap limit set in 1968 was being over-fished and needed to be revised. Last fall, these fishermen were anxious to consult with federal officials and resolve the issue, but it soon became clear that the Government did not respect the knowledge and opinions of the fishermen. The Government was determined to bring in its heavy artillery and enforce the old trap limit in spite of evidence that lobster stocks are increasing. This enforcement would ultimately keep these fishermen below the poverty line, or drive them out of business altogether.
It is not only the fishermen who are under attack but the entire social fabric of Shelburne County. The reputation of the Crown is being defiled in the process. Fisheries officers are destroying legal fishing gear and refusing to acknowledge the fact. They are also guilty of making misleading statements and of unreasonable search and seizures, harassment, and unequal application of the law. Every attempt by fishermen to resolve this issue peacefully has been contemptuously rejected. I wrote to the Minister about this on February 28-

subsubtopic: NATIVE PEOPLE FISHING FOR SALMON-INTERPRETATION BY MEDIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the last few days, there have been frequent comments on television and on the radio that Indians are overfishing salmon. I would like to say that this is not altogether true, because last November, when the Government of Canada, through the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, purchased fishing rights for the Mingan River, the Montagnais Indians in the area unanimously decided to refrain from all fishing in this river, in order to protect the salmon and evaluate fish stocks.
Mr. Speaker, what we must understand at this point is that the issue is not really the Indians' salmon fishing rights but their ownership claim on the salmon rivers.
Mr. Speaker, I think there are two things we must distinguish here. When the media tell us that the Indians refuse to observe salmon quotas, it is not the same as being told they refuse to act responsibly in this area. By fishing selectively, the Indians want to show us that they own these rivers. What the provinces must do is ensure that the Indians are given responsibility for the rivers and leave it at that. I am convinced the Indians will do exactly what they did on the Mingan River this year, where no salmon was taken at all. They are now proceeding with a scientific evaluation of the fish stocks.
Mr. Speaker, I think we should be careful when the media say the Indians are acting irresponsibly with respect to salmon fishing, because it is another case of claims being made on the basis of aboriginal rights.

subsubtopic: INCLUSION OF WORKERS' DISABILITY BENEFITS IN CALCULATION OF INCOME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is difficult enough in these hard economic times for average Canadians to live comfortably on their earnings. For our elderly living on low and fixed incomes it is virtually impossible. Our senior citizens struggle to stay alive while the Liberal Government wastes billions of Canadians' dollars on Canadair, de Havilland, Petrofina, and Maislin. Now the Liberals are trying to pay off their massive deficit on the backs of Canadians, taxing everyone and everything in sight, including the elderly.
Previously, when applying for the guaranteed income supplement, workers' compensation benefits were not counted as income, because a disability is a disability regardless of age. This year the Government decided that workers' disability benefits must be counted as income. Senior citizens who have suffered an injury on the job need and deserve the disability benefits which they effectively lose through this totally unnecessary government action.
There is a real fear among our senior citizens that this Liberal Government, insatiable in its quest for tax revenue, will directly tax workers' compensation benefits next. This must not be allowed to happen.
June 1, 1984

Mr. Speaker, the House is so quiet today I think I should make an announcement. The Department of Employment and Immigration will announce in early June a new program called the Volunteer Initiatives Program. It is for people on unemployment insurance who are unlikely to find work. It will pay $50 a week to sponsors for their overhead. I am not sure whether it will pay the people on unemployment insurance any extra money. The sponsors are charities, schools, hospitals, and some community centres.
The problem is that this program is the old Liberal shell game of job creation. You take some workers off the streets and possibly replace people who are already working full time in these voluntary organizations. The Government is again using charities to fill gaps in the Public Service. We in B.C. know what it is like when nurses are laid off and low wage, unskilled volunteers are hired to fill their place.
I have three suggestions for the Government, one, that there be a mechanism in this program to protect existing workers in agencies so that we are not just displacing existing workers. Second, more people should be eligible. People on welfare, for example, should be eligible. Third, we should look at a full-scale program of job creation, not just one more stop gap, band-aid measure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that a Conservative Member must
Oral Questions
rise to clarify a policy statement made by the Social Credit Government of British Columbia. I would draw his attention to the fact that when one begins to pump water into tanks for export purposes, one deprives the water basin of its water. In addition to that, it deprives the river of the biological role that that water plays downstream in its estuary. Thus, it affects the life forms along the shores and under the water surfaces that exist as a result of that water coming down from higher levels. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased with this opportunity to speak on second reading of the Bill to amend the Yukon Quartz Mining Act.
Although the proposed amendments are relatively minor since they concern only one section of the existing legislation, they are extremely important to the continuing stability and expansion of the mining industry in the Yukon. That is why I hope the House will expedite consideration and passage of these amendments.

Furthermore, our policy for supporting a comprehensive and ongoing program for construction of roads and industrial facilities in the North is a clear indication to prospective entrepreneurs that the federal Government is prepared to make the North's resources more accessible. Mr. Speaker, the Bill before the House today is a direct result of our concern for maintaining this climate of confidence and stability. We must deal with a situation that might create a lot of confusion in the mining industry in the North and thus preclude future resource prospecting and mining in the Yukon. Mr. Speaker, it is my intention also to speak very briefly on this Bill. The objective of the Bill is to eliminate the restriction on the number of claims that can be staked by any one individual in the Yukon Territory. The reason that restriction was enacted years ago was to prevent one person from tying up too much ground. In the early part of this century and the latter part of the previous century prospectors would go out and, once they found a showing and had perhaps done a fair amount of work on that showing, it would then be staked.
That is not the way exploration is done these days. Most of the showings that could be found fairly easily have already been found and evaluated. On the basis of regional geology, regional geophysics or geochemistry, an area is now outlined and the exploration company or prospector will go into that area. They like to have some assurance of title on that area so that a fair amount of money can be spent on detail work. Very often the large area of ground is only required for a period of one or two years while this work is being done. When more desirable areas within that region have been delineated, the rest of the ground will be let go. That is the reason that for initial stages of exploration today it is necessary that far more than eight claims, which is about 400 acres, be held by one individual or corporation for the purposes of exploration.
I would like to bring to the attention of the House one instance of what I would call miscarriage of justice resulting from the Canada mining regulations made under the Territorial Lands Act. A few years ago under that Act there was a similar restriction on the number of claims that could be staked by any one individual. What is normally done in the Yukon today, as was done in the Territories on that day, is that people would go out and stake the maximum number of claims. A friend would stake the contiguous ground and then transfer it to the person who wanted it.
In this particular instance a prospector had gone up to the Hackett River area in the Territories. A group of some 150 claims had been staked and transferred to the principal by people who had assisted him. He then auctioned that ground to a British Columbia corporation. The auction payments were not made so he took the B.C. corporation to court and tried to sue it for the moneys owing. The judge in the case in a British Columbia court ruled that no moneys were owing because the claims had been improperly staked; that the intent of the
regulations had been broken and he had in fact acquired more than the permitted number of claims.
That presumably meant that the ground was open because the claims were improperly staked in the first place. The gentleman went back and restaked over the top of the ground he had initially staked. When he tried to record these new claims with the government official he was told that he could not do that because they were validly staked already. He was not able to recover in one way and was not able to get satisfaction in another way. That is one of the worst instances I can think of in Canadian jurisprudence where somebody got a pretty bad going over by the courts.
As a .result of that case, the restriction on the number of claims which could be staked in the Territories was removed. It was a lot easier to do in that case because we were operating with regulations rather than an Act of Parliament. I am pleased to see that this type of miscarriage of justice will not now happen in the Yukon as a result of the passage of these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to speak on Bill C-44 to amend the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. One of the reasons that there is some urgency to have this Bill dealt with today is that there is a trial pending in the Supreme Court of the Yukon. It was originally set for this month but is now set for September. Under the existing piece of legislation there would have been some pretty severe ramifications for mining companies and individuals involved in the staking of claims, prospecting or mining.
The Bill currently before the House does a couple of things to amend Section 12 of the Yukon Quartz Mining Act. It removes the limit on the number of mineral claims allowed to be staked. Second, it repeals provisions respecting staking of claims by power of attorney. Third, it validates all existing mineral claims which may be deemed invalid only by reason that they were staked without prior filing of a power of attorney and/or in excess of the limit imposed by the current Section 12 of the Act.
Having staked claims and mined myself in the Yukon when I worked at Big Creek south of Carmacks for Kaiser Resources, I know what the implications would be for many individuals and companies who have made use of the Act. As you will appreciate, it is a somewhat old piece of legislation; it was passed 60 years ago. It is the wording which is creating the problems. The existing Section 12(1) reads as follows:
Subject to subsection (2), a person eighteen years of age-
As has been noted by a previous speaker, "person" is no longer the proper word to be used in terms of interpretive law. It in fact should say "individual", as is now the case in the new Section 12. It goes on to say:
-or over, may personally or by attorney-
Historically that has meant that one can stake claims or by power of attorney one can be given the right to do that for someone else and then file those claims. It continues:
It was a whole new Act.

It was supposed to modernize it but there were a number of sections of that Act that were not popular with the industry. For that reason it did not make its way through the House.
Consensus for action has been difficult to achieve because, on the one hand, the mining industry which seeks this amendment has strongly opposed other measures which were included in the Yukon minerals Bill in 1970, and, on the other hand, there has not been much enthusiasm for opening the Yukon Quartz Mining Act to make only a few changes knowing that the whole Act must be brought into the twentieth century.
The anticipated reduction in investment in mining in the Yukon, foreseen if the Act was not amended, would have caused the loss of hundreds of jobs in mining which, as all Members will know, is one of the key employers in the Territory. Opportunities in the mining industry have provided employment for decades, not only to native Yukoners and Indian people in the Territory but to many who go there from other parts of the country, as I did from northern British Columbia years ago to work in the industry.
I am pleased to have spoken to the Leader of the Opposition in the Yukon Legislature, Tony Penikett, who supports the early and quick passage of this Bill to ensure that jobs are not

Mr. Speaker, I thank the Government House Leader (Mr. Pinard) and the member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) for their courtesy. I will be very brief.
I was waiting for the briefing notes, which the Parliamentary Secretary was courteous enough to supply to us, to be dealt with, but he did not deal with the points made in those very excellent briefing notes by departmental officials. In those briefing notes, the real reasons for the changes are given which are, with respect, more accurate than those which were expounded by the Parliamentary Secretary. However, that deficiency was cured by the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) who extensively used the briefing notes of the Department in making his remarks. Therefore I need not go into those now.
I think it would be of interest to members to know that there are two methods of mining in Yukon; placer mining and what
we call hard rock. This Bill deals with the hard rock. The Yukon Placer Mining Act, which is not under discussion here, deals with the other method.
Historically, putting it into perspective, the Bill was the brainchild of a man who subsequently became a Member of Parliament. He is the late Hon. George Black, who indeed occupied the Speaker's chair during the Bennett Government of the thirties. That Act was the product of his intelligence, as was the Placer Mining Act. It has stood ever since 1924 when the Act was originally passed. This legislation has enabled the industry to function efficiently and well in Yukon.
One notable, remarkable feature about the Quartz Mining Act is that it has not been changed significantly at all in those almost 60 years since it was first passed. I am afraid that every Bill that we see coming out of this place and other levels of government has a tendency always to contain a power to regulate, a power to make regulations to achieve the purposes of the Bill. The argument of the bureaucrats always is that they may have overlooked something and must make a regulation to cover the oversight.
This Yukon Quartz Mining Act has no power to make regulations and has worked very well and efficiently for 60 years. It will interest the Member for Skeena to know that the prime reason that the 1970 legislation failed-I might add after being two years in committee-was that there was a power to make regulations. The industry, the prospectors and the mineral developers in Yukon were as certain as I am now standing here today that if that power to regulate were included in the mining legislation in Yukon, they would be suffocated, as they are being now in the Yukon placer mining industry. They are being suffocated by inspectors from the Fisheries Department and inspectors from the Department of the Environment. Not that those matters are not important, they are. We have situations where a public servant from the Fisheries Department goes to a placer miner, and speaking about his mining of gold says: "Why do you want to mine it anyway, you cannot eat it?" Then he shuts him down for one reason or another.
That kind of conduct is not expanding, as the Parliamentary Secretary said in his remarks; it is suffocating the industry in Yukon. When the Parliamentary Secretary speaks of the need to pass this Bill because of the rapid expansion of the mining industry in Yukon, he is topsy-turvy. By reasons partly attributable to government and partly attributable to international markets, there is no mining industry in Yukon now except the placer mining industry and one silver mine, not three, and that mine having only opened up less than a year ago. All the rest have been shut down. Cyprus Anvil has been shut down, Venus has been shut down and Clinton has been shut down. Again, why? Partly because of FIRA and because of the application of impossible to live with regulations made by people who do not know what they are talking about; made by people like those, again with respect, who wrote the material for the Parliamentary Secretary to which he treated us

this afternoon. The kindest thing the Parliamentary Secretary could do would be to divorce himself from the beliefs expressed in the material which he gave to us.
The mineral industry in Yukon is important not just to Yukon, it is important to Canada. We displayed that when the Cyprus Anvil mine was fully operating and exporting. It affected significantly our balance of trade. It accounted for 40 per cent of the economy of Yukon. Now it is all but shut down. All that is going on now is a stripping program, with $25 million put up by the company and $25 million put up by the Government in order, as it were, to improve the asset.
What happens when the mining industry closes down, as it has in the Yukon? The railroad closes down. The railroad is still closed down because there is no backhaul of mine products. It remains closed down and the Government, knowing that there are international elements to pull together, labour elements to pull together, industrial developments to pull together from several different areas in order to reopen Cyprus Anvil and the railroad, is not acting as the catalyst it should in order to achieve that opening.
I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that if that railroad or the Cyprus Anvil mine were in the area of Oshawa, Metro Toronto or Downsview, they would both be functioning by now. I cannot overstate the importance of the industry not being isolated to Yukon but being part of a very important asset that can be exploited to the benefit of the entire country.
Southerners really do not appreciate the richness of the asset that lies in Yukon and is affected by this legislation. Stability that amendment will bring; expansion, no. This very important amendment to Section 12 will not bring about any expansion. Expansion will be brought about by the Government addressing policy questions and solving problems that are solvable immediately. There is the question of transportation, a tied-up railroad, the question of energy rates set by a Crown corporation. We even had all-Party agreement on the Penner report, but the Government did not like it, shunted it aside and sent it over to the National Energy Board and the mine is still closed down.
What are the facts with respect to this specific amendment? Fifteen years ago when I was practising law actively I discovered the defect in Section 12 and some others, although they were certainly not as fatal as this one was. I prepared a very lengthy opinion, some 50 pages of legal opinion, for the client who eventually consented to have that opinion released to the Government.
I brought this matter to the attention of the Government some 14 years ago and asserted that, if it were not rectified, what the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) calls absolute chaos would be extant in Yukon. It takes only one case to be successful and the floodgates of overstaking and claim jumping would open. This is what this case is about to do which the Hon. Member for Skeena speaks of as being before the Supreme Court in Yukon next September.
The flaw was always there. It is vitally important that it be corrected and it is vitally important that it be made retroactive
Yukon Quartz Mining Act
to 1924 because every single mineral claim that has been staked under the provisions of Section 12 is fatally flawed by the defects. It strikes at the root of title to the holder of every mineral claim in Yukon. It throws a cloud over the operations-if it ever gets operating again, and I hope it will if the Government does the right thing-of companies such as Cyprus Anvil. It throws a cloud over the title of the operating silver mine in Yukon now, United Keno Hills, and virtually every other one that may come on stream. A change is vitally necessary. But the real reason for it is to cure a title defect. Without the change that case undoubtedly would go in favour of the interpretation of the existing legislation which this amendment is intended to cure.
I just want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary in the two or three minutes remaining, because I have finished my remarks, in the event future judicial interpreters of this legislation might get to the stage where they have to read the debates to clear up any meaning which a clause might have, whether he would give me his assurance that the changing of the word "person" to "individual" has no effect, when taken together with Section 88, in preventing partnerships, syndicates, consortia, partnerships between prospectors or companies, from acquiring mineral claims by way of transfer from the individual who stakes them under the new section.
That is my understanding of the effect. However, I think we should have the Government's assurance on the record that that is the intention, so that if we ever get that far in the judicial interpretation process it will be clear for future judges who might consider these matters.
I am sure the House would agree, Mr. Speaker, not to see the clock until the Parliamentary Secretary gives us that assurance.

that Bill C-41, an Act to implement a treaty between Canada and the United States relating to the Skagit River and Ross Lake, and the Seven Mile Reservoir on the Pend d'Oreille River be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, referred to Committee of the Whole.

speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie
speechtext:
That is the right mood for us to be in because this is a good news Bill. One of the major successes in the relations between Canada and the United States in the past year has been the satisfactory conclusion of negotiations to resolve the Skagit issue. This issue, the threatened flooding of the Skagit River Valley in British Columbia by the raising of the existing Ross Dam in the United States, has been a long-standing irritant in Canada's relations with the United States. The settlement proposal developed during negotiations involving the Canadian and American federal Governments, the Province of British Columbia and the City of Seattle, when ratified and implemented by all parties, will remove the threat of flooding, thereby ensuring that the Skagit River Valley can be treasured and enjoyed by future generations in its present natural state.
It is for these two reasons of diplomacy and environmental protection that I am very pleased to introduce into the House Bill C-41, its short title being the Skagit River Valley Treaty Implementation Act, a Bill that will provide the basis for federal support of the over-all Skagit settlement.
As my hon. friends know, this Bill is necessary to the ratification of the treaty. Essentially, it is necessary in order to authorize the export of electrical power by British Columbia for 80 years and a federal guarantee of possible financial obligations. These are the two reasons why the Bill is necessary.
The basic document in the over-all settlement is a detailed agreement between British Columbia and Seattle which reflects the long-standing position of the Government that the solution of this problem was best left to those directly involved. The federal Government, however, pledged to do all within its power to facilitate the settlement in any way possible. This the Government has done.
[ Translation]
That is why, Mr. Speaker, when negotiations began to bear on issues beyond the jurisdiction of British Columbia and the City of Seattle, the Canadian and American Governments took responsibility for settling those issues through a bilateral treaty, the Skagit River Valley Treaty. The Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) had the great honour to sign that treaty on behalf of the Government of Canada when he met with his American counterpart, Mr. Shultz, in Washington on April 2, 1984. He said at the time that it was a supportive treaty, and that is indeed what it is. In fact, on March 30 1984, representatives of British Columbia and Seattle met in Vancouver to sign an agreement which is the keystone of the Skagit River settlement.
One of the essential provisions in the British Columbia-Seat-tle Agreement is the obligation on the part of British Columbia to supply electric power to Seattle over an 80-year period from 1986 to 2066. As you may know, Mr. Speaker,
June 1, 1984

currently the National Energy Board Act restricts the authority of the Governor in Council to make regulations respecting the duration of export licences to a period not exceeding 25 years. British Columbia, therefore, could not obtain a licence under the existing Act to fulfil the province's obligations under its agreement with Seattle. In order to overcome this, the Government of Canada undertook in the Skagit River Valley Treaty to seek the authorization of Parliament through the Skagit River Valley Treaty Implementation Act to approve in this specific case the export of electrical power by British Columbia for a period of 80 years. In doing so now-and it is asking the House to authorize it-the Government of Canada recognizes that the Skagit problem requires a unique solution including an exceptional override of existing legislation.
The other provision of the British Columbia-Seattle Agreement which is supported by the Treaty and addressed by this Bill involves undertakings on the part of both the Canadian and United States federal Governments to guarantee potential financial obligations on the part of British Columbia and Seattle under their agreement. I should point out that a separate Canada-British Columbia Agreement-a fourth legal document-would ensure that the federal treasury is reimbursed fully in the highly unlikely event-I underline that because I would not want to be chastised in British Columbia for lack of faith in the financial responsibilities of the provincial government-that funds are paid out by the federal Government on British Columbia's behalf.
I would like to outline briefly for the benefit of Members, and possilby more for the benefit of students of Canadian-American relations, the background of the issue and the over-all settlement. Since the City of Seattle obtained an order of approval from the International Joint Commission in 1942 to raise the Ross Dam and thus flood the Skagit River Valley, opposition to this proposal has grown in Canada, especially in British Columbia. Early attempts to have the Commission order rescinded did not prove to be successful. However, in 1982 the International Joint Commission temporarily suspended the approval given in the 1942 order to raise the Ross Dam and established a joint consultative group on the Skagit to oversee the development of a satisfactory agreement between British Columbia and Seattle. The group was co-chaired by Commissioner Richmond Olson-who I am happy to salute in the gallery-and also by Mr. Keith Bulen from the United States. Both of those gentlemen were from the International Joint Commission. The group also included representatives of the governments of Canada, the United States, British Columbia and the City of Seattle.
In December, 1983 the group formally reached a consensus on a settlement package proposal consisting of the British Columbia-Seattle Agreement, the Canada-United States Treaty and the Canada-British Columbia agreement. The basic provision of the settlement is that Seattle agrees not to raise the dam and consequently not to flood the valley, in return for a commitment from British Columbia to supply to Seattle the equivalent electric power it would have obtained if it had raised the dam. That is the quid pro quo. In return, I
Skagit River Valley Treaty
repeat, Seattle will pay to British Columbia an amount deemed to be the equivalent of the capital cost of the dam plus an annual amount in lieu of the operation and maintenance costs of the dam. That is the basic trade off. The agreement will last for 80 years, which is the estimated life of the dam.
I provide this information to Parliament, even if Members of this House are not being asked today to approve the details, which are between British Columbia and Seattle. I would, however, like to register my admiration for what is in reality a very sensible solution, one which serves to respond to the interests of all concerned. I am particularly gratified that the International Joint Commission has again proven its value in resolving bilateral issues with the United States.
The settlement as outlined in the British Columbia-Seattle Agreement will run for 80 years. On the date the Skagit River Valley Treaty comes into force, the 1942 International Joint Commission order of approval sanctioning the raising of the Ross Dam will be terminated and a major environmental objective will be achieved. Bill C-41 is necessary if Canada is to fulfil its commitment to ensure the successful resolution of the Skagit issue. It is but a part of a settlement formula developed in an atmosphere of close co-operation with the Government of British Columbia. By adopting the Bill, Parliament will not only authorize export of electrical power and provide a recoverable financial guarantee, but it will also ensure that important provincial objectives and expectations are met by this supportive federal action.
In pressing forward with negotiations, the Government was conscious that the potential flooding of the valley was of serious concern to the House as well as to the population of British Columbia. This House has expressed, in two unanimous resolutions which were made in 1970 and 1973, its desire for a solution. Ministers of environment of this Government and former governments took an active interest in promoting a successful resolution of the Skagit issue. I know that many individual Members of the House have also sought to ensure that a satisfactory settlement be found before the valley was flooded and would want to ensure that the solution was implemented without delay.
Finally, I would also point out that the United States administration, having successfully concluded its internal arrangements concerning the settlement, is now working hard to ensure Senate ratification of the Treaty. I understand that the Treaty will be submitted to the Senate next week for its ratification. We are under a deadline to complete our ratification and implementation process. The British Columbia-Seattle Agreement cannot, of course, be brought into force until this ratification and implementation Bill has been proclaimed. If the Treaty has not been ratified by both the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States by December 31, 1984, the Agreement will not come into force and will terminate. Should this happen, the settlement will fail.
The Government of Canada is not at all confident that, if that happens, it would be able to reopen negotiations and obtain as good a settlement as it has in this particular instance. So we had better make sure that we get to church on time! Of

June 1, 1984
Skagit River Valley Treaty
course, I would not expect the opposite to happen-we will get to church on time. I believe that this House, which has already stated its desire for the kind of solution which is being proposed, will co-operate fully and ensure passage of the Bill before it adjourns for the summer. It might even do that this afternoon, if the mood remains as good as it has been up until now.

Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of his remarks the Minister indicated that this was a happy occasion in the House today. I say through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister, to Government Members, to my colleagues in the New Democratic Party, to my colleagues inthe Progressive Conservative Party and to the public of Canada, that this is indeed a happy day in the House of Commons of our country.
What we are doing today completes the last stages of a struggle which commenced many years ago to save a beautiful valley in British Columbia from being flooded as a consequence of an order made by the International Joint Commission in 1942. That order was directed to permitting Seattle City Light, a power utility, to raise its existing Ross Dam on the American side of the border, and on the lower Skagit River, to an additional height which would have resulted in flooding on the Canadian side.
One may say, well, if that happened in 1942, how did it happen if so much objection was raised many years later? It is instructive, I believe, to advise the House of the hearing, which was held in Seattle, from which the 1942 order arose. It was held in the autumn, in September of 1941. I will read from a publication produced by a group of citizens, organizations and individuals who banded together years ago to save the Skagit River. It is called "A Citizen's Guide to the Skagit Valley". On page 54 the following records what happened in 1941, and I quote:
The only opposition came from B.C. Game Commissioner J. G. Cunningham. After apologizing that "I am not familiar with the subject discussed here today ... our Commission was not on the list of those advised", he continued "I am here merely to present a brief on behalf of the sportsmen of the Skagit River. It is one of the best fly fishing streams in the whole of British Columbia ... the more of that stream you flood, the less fishing we are going to have".
The book from which I am reading continues on in the next paragraph, and I cannot help but enjoy the smile of bemused understanding on the Minister's face because he knows what is coming. It continues, and I quote:
Canada's contribution to the Commission's deliberations was a fifty word statement from Victor Meek, Controller of the Dominion Water and Power bureau, who said: "I am representing the Canadian Government, Department of External Affairs, and I have no statement to make at this time. I assume that we will have an opportunity of presenting a brief later, after we have had a chance to study the details of this project as presented this morning."
The book goes on to comment on that pious hope of a further discussion and brief-and I see the Minister smiling broadly now "He never did". So the matter, Mr. Speaker, drifted away out of the consciousness of even those few people who did attend on that momentous occasion, and for many years in British Columbia those of us who loved fly fishing,
camping and the outdoors visited the Skagit River never realizing that between the years 1941 and 1942 an order had been passed, without any public notice of any tangible degree, which, if acted upon, would take that valley forever from the people of our country.
Hon. Members of this House will know that eventually, in the passage of time, the Government of British Columbia negotiated with the Seattle City Light utility as to what should be a fair rental for the land which was to be flooded. For a long time the then Premier, the Hon. W. A. C. Bennett, would not come to an agreement with the City of Seattle because he apparently did not think it was a good enough deal.
Then something quite extraordinary happened. In 1967 British Columbia suddenly signed an agreement with the City of Seattle, and again I quote from this short but succinct history book:
Considering how long the B.C. Government had stalled Seattle's plans, the terms of the final agreement signed by B.C. Resources Minister Ray Williston on January 10, 1967 are truly astonishing. For an annual rental of U.S. $34,566.21 ... and taxes of about $10,000 per year, Seattle Light gained the right to flood 21 km of prime Canadian land and to save itself $12-15 million per year on the cost of alternative electrical power.
Therefore, Hon. Members will understand why, when this information finally became public in British Columbia, those who cared were mobilized into action. It is impossible today, Mr. Speaker, even to begin to honour, to extend our appreciation and congratulations to all those Canadians who tried so hard in those early years to mobilize public opinion and who, by their tenacity in staying with the challenge, have contributed so substantially to this moment today.
However, some of the people should be mentioned. One person is a former Liberal member of the Legislative Assembly, David Brousson. Another person is the present Premier of the Province of British Columbia, Bill Bennett. When he became Leader of the Social Credit Party, he made a political decision to try to save the Skagit River. He no doubt listened long and hard and carefully to the arguments of Mr. Brousson, who worked with other members of the Legislature, including members of the New Democratic Party, to persuade Mr. Bennett to fight to save the valley.
Another person who it would be remiss not to mention specifically is the Hon. Stephen Rogers, who was the Minister of the Environment and had an outstandingly capable Deputy Minister, Mr. Ben Marr, at the time when the most difficult negotiations were carried on with Seattle. I believe it has to be remembered that if it had not been for the conviction on the part of the Hon. Stephen Rogers that this was the right thing to do, to find a way to make an agreement with Seattle City Light and to do this in a civilized way between good neighbours who share a common border, we probably would not be discussing this Bill today.
Having mentioned these particular politicians, Mr. Speaker, it must also be recorded that men and women of all Parties with goodwill in political life, who sit in the Legislature of the Province of British Columbia and in this House, have worked
June 1, 1984

continuously for many years to be sure that a happy result would indeed come about. So I pay them tribute.
I would like to pay tribute also to the International Joint Commission. The Minister has referred to two members of that commission, one a Canadian and one an American. However, I believe for the record that we should record that when this arrangement was finally effected under the aegis of the International Joint Commission, the Hon. J. Blair Seaborn was, and is, the Canadian Chairman; Mr. E. Richmond Olsen and Monsieur Charles Bedard are the other two Canadian members. At the same time the American Chairman was the Hon. Robert C. McEwan with his commissioners, L. Keith Bulen and Donald L. Totten. I am sure that the other members of the International Joint Commission will not mind at all when I single out the Hon. Richmond Olsen and the Hon. Keith Bulen for having played a significant and at times almost dramatic part in establishing a regime and climate within which the Agreement the Minister referred to was worked out.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to record the associations which made up the ROSS Committee, which was called the Run Out Skagit Spoilers Committee. These are citizens' groups in British Columbia. The Alpine Club of Canada; British Columbia Federation of Fly Fishers; British Columbia Wildlife Federation; Dogwood Canoe Club; Federation of B.C. Naturalists; Federation of Mountain Clubs of B.C.; Langara Environmental Voice; Recreational Canoeing Association of British Columbia; Sierra Club of Western Canada; Skagit Anglers; Society for Promotion of Environmental Conservation; University of British Columbia Environmental Interest Group; Vancouver Natural History Society; and the Western Canada Wilderness Committee.
Some may have been missed. Certainly there is no way that all the individuals who helped can be recognized today. But it is also very important for everyone in this House to realize that if we had not had the dedicated help of American citizens on the other side of the line who with us wanted to save this valley, we would not have been successful. I know all Hon. Members will agree with me that we wish a tribute to be extended to all of the Americans who, over so many years, helped us in Canada to save this valley, not just for ourselves but for our children and grandchildren.
This has indeed been for me an exciting and wonderful occasion this afternoon. Dave Brousson, who I mentioned earlier, was a Liberal member of the Legislative Assembly in B.C. in the late sixties. In 1970 he came to me and asked if I would get involved. Would I be prepared as a lawyer, in my own time and at my own expense, to present a brief to the IJC. We did and that put some of the legal arguments and constitutional and international issues in the public forum. There were a great many people who worked very hard because they believed in something decent and right. They were able to persuade others that this indeed was the way to settle matters between Canada and the United States. To them I want to
Skagit River Valley Treaty
express my deep appreciation for the work which has led to this Bill being presented in this House today. I am sure that all Hon. Members will agree with me when I echo again the Minister's words, that this is indeed a happy day.

Mr. Speaker, I am honoured as well to have an opporutnity to speak very much in favour of Bill C-41. It is a happy and important day where all Members of this House can rise and take some pleasure in complimenting those hundreds and thousands of Canadians who worked so long and hard to see the Parliament of Canada pass our part of this Treaty. I am sure we all share the hope that the U.S. Senate will move expeditiously next week to pass their part of the Treaty.
There are a couple of points which the Minister touched on which I think are worth reiterating. Power will be supplied by British Columbia to Seattle for the next 80 years. What this Bill does is override part of the National Energy Board Act which allows only a 25-year maximum firm power export. It also enshrines federal Government guarantees should there be any difficulties on either side regarding any change in view by Seattle City Light on the one hand, or by British Columbia on the other. The interim agreement reached on March 30 of this year, and the Bill we are going to pass in the House today, was signed by our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and his American counterpart, Mr. Shultz, on April 2 this year. The Treaty will take us to the year 2065.
Before entering into the long history of this matter, Mr. Speaker, I want to add some kind words for the Ross committee. They worked long and hard for more than a decade to get Canada, British Columbia and the IJC moving, and to mobilize public opinion with our good neighbours in the State of Washington. I must say that wherever I went on this matter the work of the Hon. Member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser) was well known. I think that Members of the House are aware of the work he did, even though at times certain Members on the other side tried to dispel that by saying it was simply a rumour. The record shows, and those who have been involved for many years know, that his work on this matter was crucial to our being able to stand to speak in favour of this Bill today.
The history of the High Ross Dam proposal is worth putting on the record for, as the Minister would say, the students of the history of Canada-U.S. relations on matters such as this. I will try not to go back over the points touched on either by the Hon. Member or by the Minister. The original concept of the integrated development of the Skagit River hydroelectric potential was formulated by Seattle City Light back in 1906. After they looked at the area and the size of the dam required to maximize power production, the next major move was in 1929 when Seattle acquired private lands within the proposed flood basin in B.C., lots 221 and 222, which totalled about one square mile. In 1937 the Ross Dam, stage one, began, and by 1941 Seattle City Light had applied to the IJC for authority to flood Canada under the 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty.
On September 12, 1941, a hearing in Seattle lasted one hour and 55 minutes on the Seattle proposal. The Hon. Member for

June 1, 1984
Skagit River Valley Treaty
Vancouver South gave us a couple of appropriate quotations regarding that meeting. However, present at that time were only three of the six IJC Commissioners. The Canadian Chairman was absent. External Affairs was represented by a man who had not previously heard of this project and he stated that he assumed we would have an opportunity to present a brief after we had had a chance to study the details of this project as presented that morning. British Columbia, as has already been mentioned, was represented by Game Commissioner Cunningham, who was not officially notified of the hearing but simply came to talk about fly fishing for a total of about one minute.
In 1942 the IJC order of approval, giving provisional agreement for fair and adequate compensation of all interests in B.C., was concluded. The decision was taken by four of the six Commissioners, including the Canadian Chairman who had been absent at the earlier hearing. There is no known record of input by External Affairs on behalf of Canada, or by the public.
The next move in the long history of this matter was in 1947 to 1952 when there were a number of unsuccessful negotiations between Seattle City Light and British Columbia regarding compensation. Then the whole matter started to flare up in 1953 when Seattle City Light illegally flooded about one square mile of Canada's Skagit Valley line below the elevation of 1,600 feet. This was protested at the time and was subsequently covered by an interim agreement for British Columbia to receive the wonderful amount of $5,000 per annum from Seattle City Light for the flooding of a square mile of our country.
In 1967 it really started to heat up. British Columbia signed the agreement with Seattle City Light providing for the flooding of the Skagit Valley to an elevation of 1,725 feet, which is another 125 vertical feet of the valley floor, in return for an annual payment of just over $34,000 U.S. plus taxes. There was some quibbling as to how high the taxes would be. It depends upon which document you read; some say $3,000 per year and some say $10,000. Seattle was also required to clear the reservoir basin and replace the inundated sections of existing road before flooding using residents of B.C. for all the work.
It was at this point that Canadians started to realize the dilemma which had been created. The fishermen who went right down into the flood area at certain times of the year realized what was happening with the drawdown of the basin. They would see all the stumps and mud flats during the filling period, particularly early in the spring when there was some pretty good fishing. However, at that time it took most of the summer to fill the level of water up to any kind of a reasonable looking shoreline.
In 1969 there was an application for a licence by Seattle City Light and the public opposition really began. It was at that time that the ROSS Committee, the Run Out Skagit Spoilers, was formed. This group was very active for 15 years and still exists. In 1970 opposition to the High Ross Dam was
announced by the Government of Canada. As the Minister pointed out, in that year and again three years later Parliament spoke as one voice, as we occasionally do, in unanimously opposing the flooding of the Skagit Valley.
In 1971 there was a bilateral reference to the IJC with the terms of reference limiting study to environmental effects and the potential for mitigation with recommendations not inconsistent with the 1942 order of approval of High Ross. We have to reflect on what was happening during that period of time when the initial order was made in 1942. The world was at war and the meeting, as we know, was a very unusual one in that our representative of External Affairs said 50 words. Our other representative was a game commissioner who said about the same amount. It is on that original meeting in 1942 that the City of Seattle based all of the litigation and desire to flood that part of the Skagit Valley.
In 1972 the Government of British Columbia announced opposition to the High Ross. It had taken some time. Perhaps to some extent a change in government had allowed for that initial change in view within the Province of British Columbia.
From 1974 to 1977 the U.S. Federal Power Commission, which is now called FERC, held hearings leading to the approval of High Ross. At that time there was no formal intervention by British Columbia or Canada. In 1975 negotiations between B.C. and Seattle in view of settlement began. These proved fruitless and were finally suspended in 1979. In 1980, at the beginning of this Parliament, the United States Court of Appeal upheld the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission decision in favour of High Ross, rejecting inter-venors' petitions for review. I am sure that Members of the House recall that during the early days of this Parliament that matter was raised repeatedly and heatedly in the House. Various Members of the House intervened individually or as groups at that time.
On August 14, 1980 British Columbia filed a petition to the IJC requesting it to declare the 1942 order of approval a nullity. On reflection in a historical sense, I think we can all agree that in light of the circumstances of that period of the 1940s, that is something one would have hoped Seattle might have agreed to. The petition also requested the IJC to rescind the approval contained in the order, or to declare the raising of the Skagit River to an elevation of 1,725 feet contrary to the public interest of Canada and the United States, or to declare that no suitable or adequate compensation had been reached in accordance with the principles of the IJC, or to declare the 1967 compensation agreement invalid, and to direct Seattle not to flood the Skagit pending adjudication of the B.C. request.
The grounds for the request included the following: (1) That the 1941 IJC hearing was conducted by less than a majority of the Commission, and the 1942 order of approval was voted on by one member, of four voting, who had not heard the evidence, violating IJC rules of procedure and the rules of natural justice. (2) That the 1941-42 proceedings were undertaken during a state of national emergency in both countries with the
June 1, 1984

express purpose of rapidly increasing power production for military purposes, and these conditions no longer exist. (3) Failure of the Commission to consider environmental impact of the project before taking its decision. (4) That Seattle City Light illegally flooded into Canada in 1953 and no adequate compensation had been or can be afforded therefore. And finally, that the 1942 IJC order and subsequent 1967 compensation agreement effectively delegated to Seattle and B.C. the power to determine fair and adequate compensation, a power expressly reserved to the IJC by Article VIII of the 1909 Boundary Waters Treaty.
Having given a little history, I would like to restate a few of the remarks I made in an intervention to the IJC regarding the Skagit River in the fall of 1980 concerning the history of errors. I will try not to touch on the points that have already been raised by the Hon. Member for Vancouver South.
The 1942 meeting of the IJC to discuss approval of the dam consisted of four to six Commissioners, including the Canadian Chairman. Only one member actually voted to approve the application. This was against the rules of the Commission. Based on this information, the Commission's original order should be considered invalid and, in my view, is one of the fundamental justifications at that time for the full public hearings and review.
The Province of B.C. concurred in the project since there was a "state of emergency" existing in the United States and developments requiring electricity would be required. Despite these claims, no such building took place. In fact, comments from the IJC hearing in 1941 indicate an extreme vagueness in this area: "In other words ... in view of the present national emergency we do not know how much more power and what facilities are going to be required, and we want to be prepared to proceed to increase our plant to take care of that situation if it develops". That quote is from the IJC hearings in 1941.
Clearly the mood and the context in which the original order was made was that the U.S. was requesting of Canada and British Columbia a future right for potential flooding, principally for military purposes in the case of a national emergency. Clearly that has never occurred, but nevertheless the order is what they based all of their following legal arguments on.
The Commission did not consider the environmental damage to the Skagit Valley that would result from the building of the dam. However, the Ross Dam was completed in 1949. In return for allowing the dam to be built the Commission ordered that "fair and adequate compensation" be provided to B.C. Those negotiations took four more years, when Seattle City Light finally and illegally flooded 500 acres in British Columbia.
I would like now to refer to some of those who were the most active with the ROSS Committee in getting British Columbia, Canada, and to a great extent the State of Washington, Seattle City Light, and hopefully next week the U.S. Senate, all on board for what really is a momentous and important act of cooperation between our countries. The membership of the ROSS Committee who have been active since about 1969 included the Alpine Club of Canada; the B.C. Federation of Fly Fishers; the B.C. Wildlife Federation; the Dogwood Canoe
Skagit River Valley Treaty
Club; the Federation of B.C. Naturalists; the Federation of Mountain Clubs of B.C.; Langara Environmental Voice; the Recreational Canoeing Association of B.C.; the Sierra Club of Western Canada; Skagit Anglers; SPEC; the Vancouver Natural History Society; the Western Canada Wilderness Committee; and a number of others who were active or are active now.
One of their key spokespeople, along with Ken Farquuson, was Tom Perry who authored the book which was being referred to by the Member for Vancouver South. He did a phenomenal amount of work at his own cost and in his own time, not only in putting the book together and travelling extensively in the valley, but coming here to raise the consciousness of Members of Parliament in the early part of this Parliament to get moving again on this matter.
He also wrote articles such as this one, which is entitled "Hey, this Land is your Land, Too!" It appeared in Maclean's. I quote:
The issue is an environmental classic. City Light wants to raise the existing Ross Dam on the Skagit River, backing the reservoir 13 km north into B.C. Seattle would gain electrical energy worth at least $1 million annually. In return, B.C. would lose a unique river valley and get compensation of a mere $34,566 per year.
The Canadian Skagit is a flat low-elevation valley,, which is a rarity in a region dominated by high mountains. (Eighty per cent of B.C. is over 900 metres high, and 40 per cent is tundra.) The Skagit is only a two- or three-hour drive from half the population of B.C., yet it remains in public ownership, protected as a Provincial Recreation Areas. Through it flows the finest fishing and canoeing stream in the southwestern quarter of the province, and the valley's meadows support a rich diversity of wildlife, birds and rare plants unrivalled anywhere in the region. Tens of thousands of people, Americans and Canadians alike, visit the Skagit to enjoy these special values every year.
The work of people like Thomas Perry and others should not go unnoticed by the House. For some period of time during the negotiations, this Treaty looked very fragile and as though this event today and next week in the Senate might not occur. I can give examples of this by going back to newspaper articles from two years ago of which I have many. It is a very widely reported story, to say the least, particularly on the West Coast but also all across Canada.
On the Canada-U.S. page of the Vancouver Sun on March 17, 1982, the headline read: "U.S. half of Skagit Decision in Hands of Reagan Backers". The story filed out of Washington included the following:
President Ronald Reagan may as well have appointed three billy goats to guard a lettuce patch as to name the present members of the International Joint Commission to watch over the purity of boundary waters.
The commission's meeting here last week with B.C. Environment Minister Stephen Rogers, Seattle Mayor Charles Royer and their entourages led nowhere. At the end of a long day's argument, the meeting was characterized as 'helpful' which, translated from diplomatese, means nothing had been achieved.
The rest of the article is much more vicious so I will not read it. It became somewhat of a tit-for-tat situation between British Columbia and the City of Seattle, many viewing it as a situation where the then Mayor of Seattle was seen as likely trying to become the Governor of the State of Washington. All sorts of politics began to spill everywhere.

June 1, 1984
Skagit River Valley Treaty
The Province, on April 29 of 1982, ran another banner headline on the front page which read: "Seattle ready to go with Skagit Work". The story filed in Victoria reads:
Seattle will go ahead immediately with preparations for raising the Ross dam a year from now-just in case negotiations with B.C. fail, Seattle Mayor Charles Royer said Wednesday.
But it remains unclear whether Seattle has been given the green light to do so under a decision announced Wednesday by the International Joint Commission (UC).
The decision gives the picturesque Skagit Valley southwest of Hope a limited reprieve from the threat of flooding. It imposes a one-year moratorium on the flooding to allow more time for a negotiated settlement.
After this long history of difficulties and meetings that did not seem to be originally designed to come up with the conclusions they did, there was this long period of tit-for-tat particularly between the newspapers in Canada and the newspapers in Washington and other areas of the United States. It seemed that matters would likely heat up. This was evident on April 28 with another front page banner headline in The Vancouver Sun which read: "Skagit Flooding delayed a year to let B.C., Seattle Settle Dispute". In the same paper the story went on: "Seattle Mayor's Ambitions Blamed in Skagit Issue".
I will not get into all the things that went on, but from a historical perspective it is important for people to know that as well as this Parliament being united now for almost 15 years to bring about today's Treaty, many people on the U.S. side were mobilized as well because of flooding that would damage a very beautiful valley with thousand-year-old cedars and wonderful fishing areas. There was a great deal of co-operation on the American side. There is now a good deal for Seattle City Light and the people of Washington, the valley has been saved for Canadians and Americans on both sides of the border, to say nothing of the good work done by the IJC and all Parties in the House and the Canadian public.
I put my remarks on the record with respect to the friction that took place between Seattle City Light and B.C. only as a historical reminder of all the negative occurrences before we had the opportunity to stand here today. I simply conclude by saying that, as much as Members have done a great deal of work, I think we can end this debate today by going to the Committee of the Whole and passing this Bill with the knowledge that there are tens of thousands of Canadians today who have waited a long time for this important and historic occasion.

subtopic: ASIA-PACIFIC FOUNDATION OF CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH

speechtext:
Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (for the Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for Externa! Affairs), seconded by Mr. Pinard, moved: That Bill C-42, an Act to establish the Asia-Pacific Foundation of Canada, be read the second time and, by unanimous consent, be referred to the Committee of the Whole.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to propose to the House the establishment of an institution which will go a long way towards strengthening the links between Canada and the countries of the Pacific region, and to make my fellow Canadians more aware of those realities. The Asia-Pacific Foundation of Canada will also put in concrete form Canada's "Pacific" dimension from a geographical, historical, political and economic perspective. As a country which stretches far into the west, we have to look towards the East and Parliament has a unique opportunity to do that today.
For quite a few years now, Canadians have been ever more aware of the "Pacific" dimension of their country. Naturally, Canada is proud of its long-standing relations with Europe and the countries of the American hemisphere, but the last two decades have shown us the ever growing importance of our relations with countries of the Asian and Pacific region which stretches from the Pacific rim to South Asia where more than half of mankind lives.
June 1, 1984

Canada's interest in this region is multifaceted. First, we are interested in it because of our security preoccupation, our preoccupation with peace, because of trade, commerce and economic development. We are interested in this region also because it was the first to receive Canadian development assistance. You will remember the Columbo Plan, Mr. Speaker, which was the first step Canada took in aid. The Columbo Plan was for that area. The Asia-Pacific region is also important from the point of view of immigration. Last year approximately 33,000 of Canada's 78,000 immigrants came from that region. It is important also from the point of view of education. For example, 33,000 foreign students who are studying in Canada now, 53 per cent of the total number, come from the region with which we are concerned now. Finally, it is important from a cultural point of view. I think we all know how much we have gained and how much we would gain from knowing more about those great cultures of Asia which are found in that area, referring to the Indian, the Chinese and the Japanese cultures. There is so much to be learned and so much to be absorbed from this region.
The recognition of the Asia Pacific region's importance to Canada is, of course, not new. The links constituted by human ties and commercial relations extend back to before the birth of Canada as a country. We Canadians have tended not to demonstrate a sufficient consciousness of this fact, about which I think all of us would agree. It was for this reason that over ten years ago the review of Canadian foreign policy priorities highlighted the Asia Pacific region as an area of challenge and opportunity for Canada.
The developments in the Asia Pacific region impact directly, as I said a moment ago, on our security and on our prosperity. We enjoy time honoured associations with many of the countries of the Asia Pacific region through our Commonwealth links. Furthermore, many Canadians trace their family origins to this region, which today is a major and valued source of immigration. In preparing for this speech through extensive research, I found that a decade ago the trans-Pacific immigration exceeded our trans-Atlantic immigration for the first time. Some of us might not be aware of that change.
Another related element of Canada's involvement with the region and an indication of the good faith of our commitment is demonstrated by the fact that approximately 40 per cent of our bilateral development assistance flows into the area, much of it to the heavily populated countries of south Asia. Curiosity forced me to see what that figure would be; it is over $300 million.
During the past decade, two-way trade with the Asia Pacific region has multiplied six times, and Canadian exports have increased faster to that region than to any other area of the globe. Another important landmark, if I may give another one, is that in 1982 two-way trade with the countries of the Asia Pacific region surpassed our trans-Atlantic trade for the first time. The two facts that I consider to be extremely important are, first, that immigration-wise ten years ago the Pacific region became a more important source than the Atlantic
Asia-Pacific Foundation
region to our population growth, and, second, that in 1982 our trade with the Pacific area became more important than our trade across the Atlantic.
The economic dynamism of many countries in this region has been extremely impressive, but the future holds even greater promise.
Many of us in this House are envious occasionally of the growth of some of these countries. I refer, for example, to Japan and Korea in this respect.
We must foster Canada's entrepreneurial capacity to contribute to and to profit from this process. There are not only great trading opportunities, but the scope for investment, joint ventures, and technological co-operation is significant. The Secretary of State for External Affairs gave a speech in Vancouver on May 22 entitled "Canada-A Pacific Nation", in which he gave some interesting examples of these developments with the Pacific region.
It is in recognition of these salient realities that the Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan), when he was Secretary of State for External Affairs, asked Mr. John Bruk, a leading Vancouver businessman with extensive experience in Asia, to undertake a feasibility study to determine how best to enhance Canadian relations with that region. Attention had earlier focused on the concept of a non-profit independent foundation as perhaps the best vehicle to accomplish these objectives.
To examine this idea, a founding committee was created under the chairmanship of Mr. Bruk with the mandate to report to the Secretary of State for External Affairs by July 1, 1984. It is an indication of Mr. Bruk's competence and dedication that he brought in his report well in advance of that date. In reaching their conclusions, Mr. Bruk and his founding committee travelled widely within Canada and held discussions with a broad cross-section of individuals, including representatives of provincial governments, businessmen and academics and others with a strong interest in the Asia-Pacific region. The response to the founding committee's research was extremely encouraging and, in the Speech from the Throne Address in December, 1983, it was announced that the Government intended to facilitate the creation of the Asia-Pacific Foundation. This is what we are doing today.
The aims of this foundation reflect the outcome of the founding committee's extensive research. These objectives are outlined as follows: to heighten Canadian awareness that Canada is a Pacific country as well as an Atlantic country; to raise Canada's profile in the Asia-Pacific region; to increase Canadian participation in the region's economic prosperity; to focus on policy choices facing decision makers in the private and public sectors and to generate public support for new policy initiatives; to assist business to be better prepared to interchange with and be more informed about Asia-Pacific affairs; and, finally, to educate and train young people so that they will have the knowledge and skills to support Canada's future role in the Asia-Pacific area.

June 1, 1984
Asia-Pacific Foundation
The founding committee has also identified four key issues shaping contemporary relations between Canada and the Asia-Pacific region upon which the foundation is expected to focus initially. These include the dynamics of political and economic changes in that region, commercial challenges, the impact of cultural influences and the promotion of Canadian interests in a broad context. These objectives and priorities correspond to those of this Government. The Asia-Pacific Foundation is intended to act as a catalyst in the pursuit of these objectives. In some cases it will undertake programs directly. In other instances it will contract outside organizations or individuals to undertake projects.
How will this corporation, described as a private non-profit corporation with charity status, be composed and financed? The organization of the proposed foundation is to some extent a new venture in Canadian legislative experience. The structure provides for the federal Government to appoint the chairman and nine other members of the board of directors following consultation with members of the founding committee. The other 20 directors will be appointed by the board of directors itself and will include representatives from the provinces and from the non-governmental sector such as business, labour, the academic world and so on. In drafting this legislation, the Government has been guided by the desirability of giving the board the maximum possible discretion regarding its composition and function.
The Government has developed a five-year funding strategy of $5 million for the foundation, with an initial financial subvention of $1 million. It is hoped that provincial governments and the non-governmental sector will contribute to the foundation both by supporting its operations and in the financial context.
At noon I read that three provincial governments had more or less committed themselves to support the British Columbia Government not only morally but with an amount of money. If I may be indiscreet, I think the contribution from British Columbia will be as much as $200,000 a year. The Government of Ontario and the Government of Quebec have also indicated their support. As I said, I am pleased that a number of provincial governments and private sector corporations have already indicated interest in supporting the foundation.
There are three or four other points in my notes that I want to put on the record. The first is where the foundation will be headquartered. I hesitate to quote the Bill, but it refers to the principal office being in Vancouver.

What is the future of the founding committee? It has completed its work. It is hoped that some members of the committee will in the future be associated with the foundation.

I have already indicated the composition of the board, the chairman and nine others appointed by the Government following consultation with the founding committee. I believe we have before us an historic opportunity to demonstrate this House's endorsement of the present and future importance of the Asia-Pacific region to Canadians. The creation of the foundation will symbolize Canada's commitment to the region and will provide the means to enhance mutual understanding for the people of the Asia-Pacific region. Canada should greatly profit from the foundation's activities not only in terms of the commercial opportunities which it will seek to enhance but also in terms of those other human and cultural riches with which the Asia-Pacific region is so bountifully endowed.
June 1, 1984

I hope that there is a will in this House to proceed quickly. I am sure that there is, and I commend this Bill to the consideration and action of my fellow parliamentarians. I will not sit down without having thanked John Bruk again for the dedicated effort he has put into the preparation of this foundation.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to be able to speak in support of Bill C-42 today, an Act to establish the Asia-Pacific Foundation of Canada. One reason why I am proud to be here is that the Act establishing the foundation is an historic recognition of the fact that Canada is a Pacific nation. As the Minister for External Relations (Mr. Pepin) just pointed out, in terms of both immigration and trade, the Pacific region is now more important to Canada than the Atlantic region.
The second reason why I am proud to be here todayis that I can acknowledge the fact that the genesis of this initiative stemmed from the administration of the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark).
