subtopic: ASIA-PACIFIC FOUNDATION OF CANADA ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
I would thank the Hon. Member for his clarification. For the record, he said that he was not reacting to the Bill. This Bill has now been introduced and is being supported in a non-partisan atmosphere, as I am sure the Minister himself will agree.
As I was saying, the concept behind this Bill originated when the Right Hon. Member for Yellowhead was Prime Minister. At that time, the Right Hon. Member went to the Tokyo Summit and returned with the conviction that the Pacific Rim was probably the most vibrant area for Canada's immediate and long-term future. He began a series of initiatives, including the planning of a major conference to focus attention on the Pacific Rim. This initiative was carried on by the then Minister of Trade, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), and I was asked to take on the responsibility of organizing the initial work.
At that time, the concept of a foundation was strictly theoretical as being one of the many things that were worth looking into. I think it is a tribute to John Bruk that he was able to carry this forward and it is also a tribute to the parliamentary spirit in which one administration will take forward ideas which originated with another administration. We hear a lot of acrimony in the House. There are many circumstances in which initiatives taken by one Party are not instituted by the other, but this is one initiative dealing with the future of Canada and the Pacific Rim which was taken up
Asia-Pacific Foundation
by the present administration with an acknowledgement of the work that had been done previously.
I would like to say a little bit about the background of this Bill because it shows some of the work that we as a country still must do in this area. When we first began to organize the conference at which the idea of a foundation took root, we thought that it would be something that would be of major interest to the western provinces. We did not anticipate the interest in the Pacific Rim that we found existed in the country as a whole.
When dealing with the business community, we found that it had in fact long acknowleged that Canada was a Pacific nation and that the Pacific was our front door and not our back door. The business community had long acknowledged that Canada as a whole had already done marvellous work in the Pacific Rim. We found that some of our best diplomats and some of the best External Affairs and trade people had already done much productive work in the Pacific Rim.
We found that the interest in what was happening in the Pacific extended well beyond Vancouver, a city which is and hopes to remain one of the biggest and most important centres on the Pacific Rim. I should mention that in acknowledgement of that, the City of Vancouver, under Mayor Mike Harcourt, has centred its entire strategic planning for the development of the city on its Pacific Rim future.
Premier Bennett, the Premier of British Columbia, has just returned from China with glowing reports of the increasing ties that we have in the Pacific Rim. It is worth noting that the press commented on the fact that Premier Bennett, a premier who does not always have good words to say about the present administration, spoke only as a Canadian when he was in the Pacific Rim and he spoke for Canada as a whole.
The second surprise we found when doing the initial work on the Pacific Rim was that the interest in the Pacific went beyond trade. We sometimes forget that while trade is one of the most important aspects of our external relations, it is not the only one. The interest in the Pacific Rim extends beyond business ties. As the Minister has pointed out, the interest is cultural as well and involves the flow of people into Canada, the increase in our population, the desire for information about each other and the wish to travel and learn more about each other. Therefore, it is interesting to note that when describing the purpose of this foundation, the Bill acknowledges this very broad based interest. I shall read the clause in the Bill which relates to this acknowledgement. Clause 3 reads as follows:
The purpose of the Foundation is to develop closer ties between the peoples and institutions of Canada and the peoples and institutions of the Asia-Pacific region by
(a)	promoting mutual awareness and understanding of the cultures, histories, religions, philosophies, languages, life styles and aspirations in the Asia-Pacific region and Canada and their effects on each other's societies;
(b)	supporting development cooperation between organizations, institutions and associations in Canada and in the Asia-Pacific region;
(c)	promoting collaboration among organizations, institutions and associations in private and public sectors in Canada and in the Asia-Pacific region;
(d)	promoting closer economic and commercial ties between Canada and the Asia-Pacific region;

June 1, 1984
Asia-Pacific Foundation
(e)	promoting, in Canada, scholarship in and expertise on economic, cultural, social and other subjects relating to the Asia-Pacific region, and in the Asia-Pacific region, scholarship in and expertise on economic, cultural, social and other subject relating to Canada; and
{/) collecting information and ideas relating to Canada and the Asia-Pacific region and disseminating such information and ideas within Canada and the Asia-Pacific region.
As I said, the initiative for this foundation was at the government level but I think the personal initiative for this foundation lies with John Bruk. At the time he was asked to take this idea forward, Mr. Bruk was the President of Cyprus Anvil Mining Corporation. He served without any compensation for a very long time and his entire object was to promote and study the feasibility of establishing an institution to promote Canada's interests in Asia and the Pacific. His first report documented widespread interest, and in March, 1983, a founding committee was appointed. Its immediate objectives were to define the foundation's role, to set up the foundation's operating framework and to secure a broad base of funding.
It is important to note that this foundation is not one which will be funded only by the federal Government. The foundation has always worked on the belief that it should be funded one-third by the federal Government, one-third by the provincial Government and one-third by industry. The response was so encouraging and support came from such a wise cross-section of corporations and institutions that this Bill is before us today.
I should point out that the Asia-Pacific Foundation is not the first of its kind. Japan set up a similar institution more than 14 years ago. Countries such as Australia and Taiwan soon followed suit. We welcome the establishment of a nonpartisan foundation which represents all regions of the country. We also welcome increased contact and trade with Asia-Pacific. It will help us, as the Minister acknowledged, build a bridge of understanding in Canada with our many Asian neighbours in the Pacific. It will help to contribute to the Canadian cultural mosaic which makes Canada unique. It will help our Pacific neighbours understand our economic potential as a trader and become more aware of the many products and services which Canada has to offer. The foundation can help us to do all this. It is a positive step which we are taking to develop a bond of trust and mutual respect. We must work together through the foundation to make that happen. In that spirit, I am pleased on behalf of my Party to support this Bill.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on this Bill. The purpose of the Bill is to establish the Asia-Pacific Foundation of Canada. The purpose of the foundation is set out very well in the Bill. It will help to promote mutual awareness in the cultures, histories, religions, philosophies and languages of Asia-Pacific in its connections with Canada. It will help to support co-operation between organizations and groups from different sectors in the Asia-Pacific region. It will help to promote closer economic and commercial ties. It will help to promote scholarships and it will help students in the academic world in Canada to make
connections with Asia-Pacific. It will help to collect information and ideas relating to Canada's relations with Asia-Pacific.
It is important to note that the foundation could have been incorporated under the Canada Corporations Act, but we are doing it by an Act of Parliament with the co-operation of all Parties in the House. The reason for that is to show to the world and to show to our fellow Canadians the importance of this region to Canada now and in the future. As the Minister said in his speech-and it was a fine speech-the Bill shows sufficient consciousness and interest in the Asia-Pacific on the part of all Canadians.
I am pleased to speak to this Bill for the New Democratic Party and to support it. I have carried out consultations with respect to the Bill, especially with the Mayor of my city, Mike Harcourt, who, as the Hon. Member for Vancouver Centre (Miss Carney) said in her speech, has been a long-time supporter of this concept. I also spoke with Alderman Bill Yee who is a Canadian of Asian origin and who has been a supporter of this concept. I have had discussions with my own caucus and I am pleased to say that the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), for example, who does not represent the Pacific area of the country, has shown an interest in this concept. The Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) always shows an interest in exciting areas. He has also shown an interest. He lives closer to Asia than any of us. He lives in a log cabin in the Queen Charlotte Islands.
I would like to extend my thanks to another Canadian, John Bruk, who is in the Gallery today. As other speakers have said, he has done much to get this concept going and to get this Bill into Parliament. I would like to quote from a letter which Mr. Bruk, in his capacity as Chairman of the founding committee, wrote to my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). The letter is dated March 8, 1984, and reads in part:
As you know, one of the major challenges facing Canada in the coming year will be how to react to the emergence of the Asia-Pacific region as a principal economic and political power. Therefore, there is a pressing need for greater emphasis in making Canadians fully aware of the growing importance of our trade with the Asia-Pacific region, as well as raising Canada's profile in those countries and enhancing the skills and understanding of Canadians doing business within the region.
Moreover, we must ensure that the next generation of Canadian political and business leaders and the general public have an even greater understanding of Canada's opportunity in the Asia-Pacific region.
When I was entering this House to speak today I said to the pages: "You should listen to some of our speeches because in a few years you will be learning Mandarin". One of the pages told me that, indeed, he will be starting a course in the Chinese language, as I am this summer. I will speak in French later on and I am sure the Minister will say that perhaps I should spend my time working on French. However, I think that the letter from Mr. Bruk hits the nail on the head with respect to why we are incorporating this Bill.
I think we must understand what is happening in the most dynamic growth area of the world, that is, the Asia-Pacific. Some statistics were given by the Minister. I would like to quote from the Chinatown News. The editor of the Chinatown
June 1, 1984

News, Mr. Roy Mah, has been very active in promoting this concept. He wrote an editorial on April 3, 1984, which reads in part:
Canada is a Pacific nation as much as an Atlantic one. Increasingly it is Asia which supplies our immigrants and purchases our goods. Last year, Asia provided 40 per cent of the new arrivals in Canada, compared to only 29 per cent of European origin. The Asian markets absorbed a record $8.6 billion worth of Canadian goods, while Canadian exports to Western Europe-worth $10.1 billion as recently as 1981-slipped to $7.5 billion.
Mr. Mah writes further on in the editorial:
It is important that we expand the pool of businessmen, civil servants, scholars and communicators who understand the cultures, languages, politics and markets of Asia.
He is right. Many of us in the House have had a chance, during this session of Parliament, to visit Asia. The Hon. Member for Ottawa-Vanier (Mr. Gauthier) was with me when a parliamentary group visited China last fall. On that trip we saw a joint venture. In Shanghai there was a joint steel mill which was built by joint venture between Japan and China. I hope that someday that will happen between Canada and China. I have had a chance to visit Hong Kong, the Philippines and South Korea, which are only a few places in the Asia-Pacific. When Members of this House return from those trips, they say they are impressed with the dynamic nature of the region.
It was mentioned in the Chinatown News that Canada's trade with the region has exceeded European trade for the first time. Japan is our number two trading partner and Korea is our number five trading partner. We are just beginning to get into the Asia-Pacific area. We are still Euro-centric. That is only natural. We still look to Europe because, given our background, many of us have come either directly from Europe, or our ancestors have come from Europe. As well, Canada has played a very important role in Europe. It has played an important role in institutions, labour, defence, research, business, politics and so on, which I think has been of mutual benefit both to Europe and to Canada. Now we are saying-and I think this is what the Asia-Pacific Foundation is saying as well-that we have to play the same kind of role in Asia. First, however, we must have a better understanding of Asia. The foundation will help in that respect. Second, there will have to be more involvement in Asia.
The opportunities are great. I gave the example of the steel mill in China. China has decided as a matter of policy that by the year 2000 it will quadruple its Gross National Product. That means that one billion people will be quadrupling their Gross National Product. What a task! Canada will be able to help with that task. After all, Canada is a large country as well. We have learned to tame hydro power in Canada. We have had to, in order to produce electricity. We have learned to transport materials over long distances. We have opened up mines in harsh terrain. All these things Canadians can do and do very well. So there is an opportunity for the railway technology, hydro technology and mining technology of Canada vis-a-vis China.
Asia-Pacific Foundation
Right now, Mr. Speaker, a Canadian engineering firm is developing a gold mine in China. We feel that these are bitter days when we see our people a bit depressed about the future because of the high unemployment rate in Canada. But what an opportunity we have. One of the Clerks of the House, who is sitting here today, was with us in China and we all could see the possibilities for Canada to play a role in the future of China. And not only in China but in Singapore and in the Philippines. We must, however, be honest about it. While there are opportunities, there are risks as well.
We should look at some of these risks. Our trade in fact is growing rapidly in the Pacific but-and the Minister might be interested in this-our trade is not growing at the same rate as in Australia or Japan. So we do have a lot to do and we have to deal with some very difficult problems which are coming out of the Asia-Pacific.
Take, for example, the low wage countries and the competition for our textiles. There are the low economic zones with low wages, bad working conditions and poor environmental and safety standards which we see in Southeast Asia. We must be honest about it. These are some of the concerns of our Party, as well as the concerns of other Hon. Members of the House. However, we must understand these conditions before we can deal with them. We should welcome the opportunity to open up our knowledge in that area.
The Hon. Member for Skeena and I myself have struggled with this problem. We in British Columbia live with the external trade policies of Japan. It often pursues a policy of oversupply of natural resources. So we open up northeast coal in British Columbia in competition with our southeast coal, or in competition with the Australian or Chinese coal mines, all at the bidding of Japanese policy. I am not knocking the Japanese policy. I am not even knocking the different coal projects in Canada. What 1 am saying is that we must understand what the Japanese policy is so that we can have an informed debate as to what our policy should be. I do not believe we have had a very informed debate up to now on, for example, northeast coal and other projects in British Columbia, and that is the challenge of the future. These issues have to be brought into the open. These are the risks we take in dealing with Asia-Pacific.
The biggest risk of all, Mr. Speaker, it seems to me, is not understanding what is happening in this dynamic area and not taking advantage of our opportunities; and the Minister alluded to this. I do not believe we have truly recognized the dynamism of the Asia-Pacific region and we have not yet found our niche in that region. It is not just a problem or an opportunity for those of us in British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, I have already said that the new Asiatic markets are important to my own Province of British Columbia, but other Canadian provinces will have to get more enthusiastically involved in trade with the Asian and Pacific countries. I am referring to Quebec particularly because there

June 1, 1984
Asia-Pacific Foundation
is a francophone culture in the Pacific region-Tahiti, New Caledonia and others-and there are always people who speak French in the former French colonies of Southeast Asia. Quebecers might take advantage of that common linguistic heritage to seek new markets for their own products. True, the principal office will be in Vancouver, but it will serve Quebec as well.

It is very important, Mr. Speaker, that all regions of Canada have an interest in this. We must understand the Asia-Pacific. One of the ways in which we might do that lies right under our own noses; that is, that we have Canadians of Asian origin who do understand the languages, cultures and the business of Asia-Pacific. We should mobilize this Canadian talent. We should lay a foundation as a means of mobilizing that talent. I have only very recently formulated this thought in my own mind-although I am sure it is an old one-but I believe it is an answer to those of us on the Pacific coast who struggle with the problems of discrimination against new immigrants and the problems of racism, which is inherent, I must say, in parts of Canada. Our history proves that. However, there is also a good side to Canadians. It occurred to me, and I believe it has occurred to other people as well, that we have this multicultural aspect of Canada, which makes us credible to the Pacific nations. They see us as a peaceful people, a people of different backgrounds, many of whom are from Asia-Pacific and who have learned to live and work together. They see the French and the English people of this country living and working together, and they are seeing other Europeans living and working peacefully with Canadians. They can also see Europeans and Asians all living together peacefully as Canadians. That gives us a tremendous advantage and we should work on that advantage. Therefore, I ask my fellow Canadians to open up our collective eyes and to work from our strength, to use our people of Pacific origin in a much better way in order to help us understand the land of their forefathers, the Asia-Pacific.
How do we raise Canada's profile in Asia? The Bill talks about the role of the foundation; an exchange of scholars; visiting students; selected conferences and publishing programs which are in place already. For example, Mr. Speaker, it was just announced that the school system in British Columbia is offering Japanese and Chinese as optional languages. That is a real step forward taken by the Social Credit Government. The Simon Fraser University, UBC and UVIC are planning to establish a centre for Asian Pacific studies in the new Canada Harbour Place in British Columbia. That is another step forward. This foundation will be able to publicize these initiatives, taking that message to Asia.
The Minister has already spoken about the foundation, so I will not say too much about it. However, I will say that its responsibility is split in three ways: the federal Government, the provinces and the private sector. Private sector does not only mean business, I hope. It also means labour, students, young people and the academia, and that is very important. I am confident that the first directors of the foundation will
keep that in mind. It is important that we get the youth involved.
I am proud that the foundation is going to have its head office in Vancouver. Recently the Vancouver City Council has twinned Vancouver with Canton, Kwangtung. That is a small step but it is a step forward.
I would like to conclude by saying that we are a bridge to the Pacific community, quite literally. We are a bridge between Europe and the Pacific. We are now truly a country which is both of the Atlantic and of the Pacific. This Bill, passed today on a quiet Friday afternoon, is a historic symbol and augurs well for the future. It is important not only for trade and jobs, but for world peace as well. If we can duplicate in the Pacific the efforts we have made in Europe, as I believe we can, we will be a positive force there. We can mobilize our human resources, our people from the Asian Pacific and here in Canada, to help us. Asia's coming of age is among the most significant themes of the remaining years of this century. The Asia-Pacific Foundation, through its organization of conferences, publications, information bank and promotion of educational and cultural exchanges, will bring us significantly closer to understanding Asia and will also help Asia to better understand us.
There is a Chinese symbol for crisis, Mr. Speaker, consisting of two components. The top character signifies danger, and the bottom character signifies opportunity. I think it is time to seize that opportunity, and this is what this Bill does. I think it was Confucius who said that you have to begin a journey of 1,000 miles by taking the first step, and I think we have taken that first step today in turning Canada into becoming increasingly a Pacific nation and taking advantage of the great opportunities in that region for Canada.

Leasing of Crown Lands

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEASING OF CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time I would like to thank the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) for the assistance and co-operation which he and his office have given to this matter over quite a few years. I would also like to thank the House Leaders from the various Parties for allowing this Bill to proceed expeditiously this afternoon.
When I introduce this Bill I do so with a certain sense of embarrassment. If this Bill is passed into law, the advantages which will accrue therefrom will be most advantageous to those Members who live in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. There are not very many of us. There are three Members of Parliament and two Senators. The problem which this Bill addresses is that under Section 20 of the Senate and House of Commons Act as it stands today, due to inadvertency Members of Parliament and Senators are prevented from leasing federal Crown lands. In the Yukon and the Northwest Territories, apart from a very small amount of privately owned land in municipalities, all the rest of the land is federal Crown land. That means that Members of Parliament from those Territories are unable to lease a cottage lot or acquire any land outside of privately owned land within the municipalities. I do not think that was the original intent of Section 20 when it was drafted. The intent was to prevent Members of Parliament from entering into contracts with the federal Crown from which they might derive pecuniary benefit.
Because I stand to benefit from this more than most Members of Parliament, I took the precaution of writing in advance to the Speaker of the House of Commons in 1980 when the Hon. Jeanne Sauve was Speaker. I asked whether it would be proper for me to introduce such an amendment. In a letter dated July 2, 1980 I was told that it would be in order for me to do so and I would not be contravening any of our rules in doing this.
I will return to the recent history of the need for an amendment. On May 14, 1970 the Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) rose on a point of privilege in the House and brought to the attention of the House the fact that he had been trying to acquire a cottage lease in the Yukon where he resided and had been turned down because of the provisions of Section 19, as it then was, of the Senate and House of Commons Act. As a result of his intervention on that day, the matter of his acquisition of a lease was referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections, which duly convened to discuss the matter. It held a couple of meetings and issued a report which was tabled in the House of Commons on June 3, 1970.
The principal recommendations of the committees were as follows:
1.	The question of privilege is well founded.
2.	Your Committee, being of the opinion that as there may exist similar cases involving other Members of the House, recommends that the same considerations and recommendations should be made applicable in these cases.
3.	Your Committee recommends that the Government should consider the expediency of introducing legislation to amend the Senate and House of Commons Act to resolve more clearly the question of the propriety of Members of Parliament receiving certain payments and advantages under Acts of general application and of Members making payments for leases, rent or sale of property in certain cases where they do not receive any special or undue advantages simply from the fact that they happen to be Members of Parliament.
The committee also recommended that the particular lease in question be granted. The report of the Committee on Privileges and Elections was concurred in by the House of Commons on June 10, 1970.
In my own case I have run up against Section 20, as it now stands, by virtue of the fact that before entering into politics I was a prospector and acquired, through staking, mineral claims in the Northwest Territories. A provision of the Canada mining regulations is that within a 10-year period a claim must be taken to lease. I was unable to obtain a lease because of the Senate and House of Commons Act and, therefore, property which I had previously acquired was in jeopardy.
The change which is proposed to the Act is a very simple one. I propose to read Section 20(1) as it now stands and insert the change. The sub-section reads:
In every contract, agreement or commission to be made, entered into or accepted by any person with the Government of Canada or any of the departments or officers of the Government of Canada-
We now come to the insertion:
-for which any public money of Canada is to be paid-
Now we go back to the old wording:
-there shall be inserted an express condition that no member of the House of Commons shall be admitted to any share or part of such contract, agreement or commission, or to any benefit to arise therefrom.
It is a very simple change. It would not change the Act in such a way that Members of Parliament could enter into contracts for the provision of services to Government, or enter into contracts where money would be paid by the Government to the Member of Parliament. Rather, it would only apply the other way around, where a Member of Parliament pays money to the Crown.
I think that is a sufficient explanation of the changes which are proposed. I would again like to thank the other Parties, and particularly the President of the Privy Council for the co-operation and worthwhile advice they have given with respect to this matter over many months, if not years. I think it has taken that long.

Mr. Speaker, I only have a few brief remarks to make in support of Bill C-241. I recognize the dilemma in which the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) finds himself. While it may appear that we are taking the time of the House to pass legislation that only benefits that Hon. Member, upon close examination of old Section 20(1) of the Senate and House of Commons Act, one can see that it may well affect others besides the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), the Hon. Member for Western Arctic or the Hon. Member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar). If one is to reflect on exactly what the wording means, for those Members of the House who may want to rent a cottage lot in Banff National Park it would not be legal according to a strict interpretation of the section as it exists today. If one were to read the section even more rigidly, one might suppose that even the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau)

house, Stornoway, or other matters directly related to federal properties would be included, because Section 20(1) states:
In every contract, agreement or commission to be made, entered into or accepted by any person with the Government of Canada or any of the departments or officers of the Government of Canada, for which any public money of Canada is to be paid, there shall be inserted an express condition that no member of the House of Commons shall be admitted to any share or part of such contract, agreement or commission, or to any benefit to arise therefrom.
I presume it has been many years since someone has been confronted by such a technical situation. Clearly, the Hon. Member for Western Arctic was the first Member to really run afoul of it, one might say.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Yukon was the first. However, perhaps it is more clearly defined for the Hon. Member for Western Arctic. Although he is required in the Northwest Territories by law to proceed within ten years in order to gain title to the claims he staked out, in order to get leases on those claims, he is expressly forbidden to do that by an Act of the House. This Bill is important in terms of what has happened to the Hon. Member for Yukon and the Hon. Member for Western Arctic.
When the Parliamentary Secretary rises to speak, he will also point out that if this action were clearly interpreted and applied, its application would be found to be extremely broad. It could in fact cause a chaotic situation for many Members who, with their own money and without gaining any particular gain in relation to the activities of the House, federal law, contracts or grants, may have wanted to purchase a cottage lot but have not been allowed to do so since Confederation.
The words that have been added make it very clear that that is not the case. The words that are added in the section are simply, "for which any public money of Canada is to be paid".
It is quite clear that the passage of this Act will not bring any specific monetary, legal or other gains to the Hon. Member for Western Arctic, the Hon. Member for Yukon or other Members of the House. It is simply an attempt to make this section of the Senate and House of Commons Act clear so that Hon. Members in the future do not lose an opportunity to get a cottage lot whether it is in Banff National Park or the Pacific Rim. In the case of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic, it will allow him to deal legally with mining claims that he legally holds and must do something about.
I am pleased to rise and support this Bill. I trust that it will go through all three stages and become law today. I am sure that the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Evans) will probably want to join with me in saying that perhaps we should make one further amendment to the Senate and House of Commons Act, which is, perhaps, to abolish the Senate. However, I will leave it to you to decide, Mr. Speaker, whether you wish to rule that amendment in order. I am sure there are Members here this afternoon who

speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PUBLIC BILLS   SENATE AND HOUSE OF COMMONS ACT AMENDMENT RESPECTING LEASING OF CROWN LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am quite sure the Chair would find that particular suggestion out of order.
I too rise to support the Bill. The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) and his office have certainly worked very closely with the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) on this particular matter. It is a situation that should have been corrected some time ago.
To my knowledge, the first person to run afoul of this section was the Hon. Member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) as a result of a lease on a cottage lot in the Yukon Territories. It was raised as a matter of privilege in the House of Commons and taken before the Privileges and Elections Committee. It was found in 1970 to be clearly a breach of the laws.
That situation is to be corrected permanently by what we are doing today. As the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) has mentioned, this is much broader than just the coverage that one would find in the Northwest Territories or Yukon. It also covers many areas that one would think should not be covered in such a provision. For example, the National Capital Commission owns a good deal of land in the City of Ottawa and the National Capital Region. If a Member of Parliament were to lease a cottage lot at Meach Lake or Gatineau Park, of which there are some, that would technically be a breach of the Act as well. If a Member of Parliament were to rent an apartment on Sussex Drive on some of the land and restored buildings that are owned by the NCC, the Member would be in breach of the Act.
It is clear that there are some very serious difficulties with this particular provision. The law officer of the Crown has given the advice that the original intent of Section 20 of the Act was to ensure, as the Hon. Member for Western Arctic said, that a Member of Parliament did not engage in contracts, or transactions which would result in his or her receiving remuneration from the Crown. As the Hon. Member rightly pointed out, the effect of the amendment that the Hon. Member is putting forward today is to clarify that it applies in all cases in which a Member of Parliament was receiving benefit from the Crown in exchange for goods or services, but does not apply in cases where the Crown is receiving remuneration from a Member of Parliament for the lease of land or goods.
I suppose, according to this Act, if a Member of Parliament went to Crown Assets Disposal and bought a used filing cabinet, it would constitute a transaction between a Member of Parliament and the Crown. Prior to this amendment, it would be a matter that could be raised as privilege in the House. It would be in violation of the Act.
I am confident that there have been many Members of Parliament in the past who, like members of the general public, have gone to Crown Assets Disposal, which is in my riding, to buy a chair for an office or a filing cabinet. I am
